position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreationists, using the 406 MHz distress beacon technology. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., 5,000 units) and a direct-to-consumer sales channel, priced at €300. Use the test results to decide whether to scale or pivot to an agency-focused model.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand into a new B2B segment (e.g., commercial fishing or recreational boating) with a specialized distress-beacon solution.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (ships, aircraft, military/commercial marine).
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a necessary safety tool that provides confidence in remote environments.
T1.who_benefits: Hikers, climbers, kayakers, and other outdoor recreationists who travel in remote or dangerous areas.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of remote-area risks and a willingness to invest in safety equipment that can save lives.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers or through outdoor retailers, earning premium prices and capturing recurring revenue through accessories and service contracts.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. remained stable or increased in 2002.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a distress beacon that operates on a widely recognized frequency.
Regulatory approval (FCC waiver) makes the technology usable for distress purposes.
predictions: If offered at a price point below €300, at least 5% of surveyed outdoor recreationists would express intent to purchase.
Willingness-to-pay surveys would show average price sensitivity of €200-€300 for a distress beacon.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a necessary safety tool that provides confidence in remote environments.

T2.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they need a standardized, reliable frequency for remote location detection, and the technology reduces false alarms.
T2.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, coast guards, and emergency response teams that operate in remote or difficult-to-reach areas.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The need for a widely accepted distress frequency that can be detected across large geographic areas, combined with the ability to distinguish genuine distress signals from other signals, motivates agencies to adopt the technology.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons to government agencies and emergency management bodies through procurement channels, earning higher margins and potentially securing long-term contracts for service and maintenance.
assumptions: Emergency response agencies have budget allocations for new distress equipment in 2002.
The 406 MHz frequency is recognized as the international standard for distress beacons.
Agencies prioritize reliability and interoperability over price.
predictions: If offered to agencies at a price point of €1,500 per unit, at least 10% of surveyed agencies would express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Agency procurement officers would cite the need for a standardized distress frequency as the primary reason for selection.
T2.first_claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they need a standardized, reliable frequency for remote location detection, and the technology reduces false alarms.

assessments.does_not_show: It does not show that outdoor recreationists specifically would purchase the device, nor that they view it as a necessary safety tool.

X1.name: Consumer vs Agency Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) and 250 emergency responders/search-and-rescue personnel.
X1.measure: Percentage of each group willing to purchase the 406 MHz beacon at a price point of €300 (outdoor group) and €1,500 (emergency group). Secondary measure: average willingness-to-pay in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor group willingness to purchase ≥ 25% at €300.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency group willingness to purchase ≥ 15% at €1,500.

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor group willingness ≥ 25% and emergency group willingness ≥ 15%, proceed with consumer launch (supports T1). If emergency group willingness ≥ 20% and outdoor group willingness < 10%, proceed with agency-focused launch (supports T2).

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreationists, using the 406 MHz distress beacon technology. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., 5,000 units) and a direct-to-consumer sales channel, priced at €300. Use the results of the proposed Consumer vs Agency Purchase Intent Test to decide whether to scale or pivot to an agency-focused model.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who travel in remote or dangerous areas and need a reliable distress signal.
final.value_proposition: A portable, easy-to-use 406 MHz distress beacon that provides confidence and peace of mind in remote environments, meeting the FCC’s requirement for mandatory registration and the industry’s recognition of the frequency for distress.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Agency Purchase Intent Test (500 respondents, €18,000, 10 weeks) to measure willingness to purchase at €300 and €1,500, and decide whether to proceed with a consumer launch or an agency-focused launch.
final.uncertainty: The size of the outdoor recreation market in 2002 and the willingness to pay €300 for a distress beacon are uncertain. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows <10% willingness to purchase at €300 among outdoor recreationists, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore other B2B segments or licensing the technology.

arguments.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a necessary safety tool that provides confidence in remote environments.
arguments.who_benefits: Hikers, climbers, kayakers, and other outdoor recreationists who travel in remote or dangerous areas.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of remote-area risks and a willingness to invest in safety equipment that can save lives.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers or through outdoor retailers, earning premium prices and capturing recurring revenue through accessories and service contracts.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. remained stable or increased in 2002.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a distress beacon that operates on a widely recognized frequency.
Regulatory approval (FCC waiver) makes the technology usable for distress purposes.
predictions: If offered at a price point below €300, at least 5% of surveyed outdoor recreationists would express intent to purchase.
Willingness-to-pay surveys would show average price sensitivity of €200-€300 for a distress beacon.

arguments.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they need a standardized, reliable frequency for remote location detection, and the technology reduces false alarms.
arguments.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, coast guards, and emergency response teams that operate in remote or difficult-to-reach areas.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: The need for a widely accepted distress frequency that can be detected across large geographic areas, combined with the ability to distinguish genuine distress signals from other signals, motivates agencies to adopt the technology.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons to government agencies and emergency management bodies through procurement channels, earning higher margins and potentially securing long-term contracts for service and maintenance.
assumptions: Emergency response agencies have budget allocations for new distress equipment in 2002.
The 406 MHz frequency is recognized as the international standard for distress beacons.
Agencies prioritize reliability and interoperability over price.
predictions: If offered to agencies at a price point of €1,500 per unit, at least 10% of surveyed agencies would express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Agency procurement officers would cite the need for a standardized distress frequency as the primary reason for selection.

arguments.quote: The 406 MHz PLB is primarily intended to provide a distress and alerting capacity for use by the general public in life threatening situations in a remote environment after all other means of notifying SAR responders (e.g., telephone, radio) have been exhausted.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that outdoor recreationists specifically would purchase the device, nor that they view it as a necessary safety tool.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Agency Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay questions.
arguments.sample: 500 respondents: 250 outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) and 250 emergency responders/search-and-rescue personnel.
arguments.measure: Percentage of each group willing to purchase the 406 MHz beacon at a price point of €300 (outdoor group) and €1,500 (emergency group). Secondary measure: average willingness-to-pay in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor group willingness to purchase ≥ 25% at €300.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency group willingness to purchase ≥ 15% at €1,500.

arguments.decision_rule: If outdoor group willingness ≥ 25% and emergency group willingness ≥ 15%, proceed with consumer launch (supports T1). If emergency group willingness ≥ 20% and outdoor group willingness < 10%, proceed with agency-focused launch (supports T2).

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.target_customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who travel in remote or dangerous areas and need a reliable distress signal.
arguments.value_proposition: A portable, easy-to-use 406 MHz distress beacon that provides confidence and peace of mind in remote environments, meeting the FCC’s requirement for mandatory registration and the industry’s recognition of the frequency for distress.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Agency Purchase Intent Test (500 respondents, €18,000, 10 weeks) to measure willingness to purchase at €300 and €1,500, and decide whether to proceed with a consumer launch or an agency-focused launch.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the outdoor recreation market in 2002 and the willingness to pay €300 for a distress beacon are uncertain. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows <10% willingness to purchase at €300 among outdoor recreationists, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore other B2B segments or licensing the technology.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a limited pilot (as proposed) to test demand for outdoor recreationists before committing resources. If the pilot meets the 15% pre-order threshold for outdoor recreation, proceed with a consumer launch; otherwise, focus on existing B2B markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand into a new B2B segment (e.g., commercial fishing or recreational boating) with a specialized distress-beacon solution.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (ships, aircraft, military/commercial marine).
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote travel, and they are willing to pay a premium for a reliable emergency device that can be used in life-threatening situations.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, climbers) who need emergency communication in remote areas.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increasing awareness of remote travel risks and the need for rapid SAR response leads users to seek certified emergency beacons that can be detected by satellites.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell premium-priced, certified beacons directly to consumers through outdoor retailers and online channels, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Consumers perceive 406 MHz beacons as a critical safety item for remote activities.
There is sufficient market awareness and trust in the technology by 2002.
Outdoor retailers are willing to stock and promote a new consumer product.
predictions: If offered at a price point of $300-500, at least 10% of surveyed outdoor recreationists would express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales in the first year would be sufficient to cover the €20,000 test budget for a limited launch.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote travel, and they are willing to pay a premium for a reliable emergency device that can be used in life-threatening situations.

T2.claim: Emergency services and search-and-rescue organizations will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they need reliable, satellite-detectable signals for remote incident locations, and they will purchase them through existing procurement channels.
T2.who_benefits: Emergency management agencies, SAR teams, and government procurement offices that require certified emergency communication devices.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of remote incident risks and the need for rapid, satellite-based detection drives demand for standardized, compliant beacons that can be integrated into existing response protocols.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell bulk, compliant beacons to government agencies and SAR contractors at lower margins but with predictable volume, leveraging existing B2B relationships and compliance certification.
assumptions: Emergency services prioritize satellite-detectable distress signals for remote operations.
Procurement processes allow direct purchase of certified equipment.
There is sufficient budget for additional emergency communication devices in 2002.
predictions: If offered at a price point of $250-350 per unit, at least 20% of surveyed emergency services would express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales in the first year would be sufficient to cover the €20,000 test budget for a limited pilot through government contracts.
T2.first_claim: Emergency services and search-and-rescue organizations will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they need reliable, satellite-detectable signals for remote incident locations, and they will purchase them through existing procurement channels.

assessments.quote: The 406 MHz PLB is primarily intended to provide a distress and alerting capacity for use by the general public in life threatening situations in a remote environment after all other means of notifying SAR responders (e.g., telephone, radio) have been exhausted.
assessments.does_not_show: It does not show that outdoor recreationists specifically adopt the beacons, nor that they are willing to pay a premium price.

X1.name: Consumer vs Emergency Services Pilot
X1.method: Run a limited pilot offering two versions of the 406 MHz distress beacon: (1) a consumer-oriented model priced at $400-500, marketed through outdoor retailers and online channels; (2) an emergency services model priced at $300-400, marketed through government procurement channels and SAR contractors. Track pre-orders or purchase intent within 12 weeks.
X1.sample: Target 200 outdoor recreationists (hiking, camping, climbing) in the U.S. via outdoor retailer partnerships and online ads, and 150 emergency services personnel (SAR teams, fire departments, police) via procurement contacts.
X1.measure: Number of pre-orders/purchase intent for each version within 12 weeks.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreationists will generate at least 15% of total pre-orders, with a total of at least 30 pre-orders.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency services will generate at least 20% of total pre-orders, with a total of at least 30 pre-orders.

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor recreation pre-orders >= 15% of total and >= 30 pre-orders, proceed with consumer launch. If emergency services pre-orders >= 20% of total and >= 30 pre-orders, proceed with emergency services focus. If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, adoption, or willingness to pay for 406 MHz distress beacons. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a limited pilot (as proposed) to test demand for outdoor recreationists before committing resources. If the pilot meets the 15% pre-order threshold for outdoor recreation, proceed with a consumer launch; otherwise, focus on existing B2B markets.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, climbers) who need emergency communication in remote areas.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced, certified 406 MHz distress beacon that provides reliable satellite detection for remote distress calls, sold through outdoor retailers and online channels.
final.next_action: Run the proposed pilot with 200 outdoor recreationists and 150 emergency services personnel, track pre-orders within 12 weeks, and decide on launch based on thresholds.
final.uncertainty: Demand for a consumer product is uncertain due to lack of pre-market evidence; willingness to pay a premium price is also unknown. Emergency services demand is equally uncertain due to procurement constraints and existing compliance paths.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows outdoor recreation pre-orders >= 15% of total and >= 30 units, indicating sufficient consumer demand.
If the pilot shows emergency services pre-orders >= 20% of total and >= 30 units, indicating a viable bulk B2B opportunity.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand into a new B2B segment (e.g., commercial fishing or recreational boating) with a specialized distress-beacon solution.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (ships, aircraft, military/commercial marine).
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

Participants are randomly assigned to view one version and then asked about purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?" ) and willingness to pay (open amount).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults: 250 outdoor recreationists (hiking, camping, climbing) recruited via outdoor activity forums; 250 recreational boat/fishing operators recruited via marine industry newsletters. Stratify by age and gender to reflect typical user demographics.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and average willingness-to-pay (EUR) for each version.

result.excerpt: (ACR) and McMurdo Limited (McMurdo) for waiver of the Commission's rules to permit the type certification of a new 406 MHz personal emergency position indicating radiobeacon (EPIRB), for the reason that the rule changes we adopt today appear to permit the equipment proposed by ACR and McMurdo.

arguments.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, low-cost emergency solution for remote activities, and ACR can capture value by selling directly to consumers at premium prices.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, climbers) who need emergency communication in remote areas.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of outdoor safety risks and the availability of a satellite-based distress beacon that does not require a phone signal or network connectivity.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR sells the beacon directly to consumers at a price point above existing PLBs, leveraging its existing 406 MHz technology and brand reputation for marine safety.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. were stable or growing in 2002.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a distress beacon that works in remote areas.
ACR can reach individual buyers through retail or online channels.
predictions: If ACR launches a consumer-focused 406 MHz beacon, purchase intent among outdoor recreationists will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable PLB.
Average price paid per unit will be at least 20% above the price of existing PLBs.

arguments.claim: Commercial fishing and recreational boating operators will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a compliant, reliable emergency solution that reduces search and rescue costs and regulatory burden, and ACR can capture value by selling through marine distributors and offering bundled services.
arguments.who_benefits: Commercial fishing vessels and recreational boats that need to meet safety regulations and reduce the risk of costly false alarms.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Growing regulatory pressure to equip vessels with approved distress beacons and the economic incentive to minimize false alarm costs.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR sells beacons through marine distributors and offers optional service contracts (e.g., registration, tracking, data analysis) that generate recurring revenue.
assumptions: Commercial fishing and recreational boating fleets in the U.S. were expanding or stable in 2002.
Operators are willing to invest in technology that reduces regulatory compliance costs.
ACR can reach marine distributors and provide technical support for B2B sales.
predictions: If ACR launches a 406 MHz beacon targeting commercial fishing and recreational boating, purchase intent among operators will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable PLB.
Average price per unit will be at least 15% above the price of existing PLBs, reflecting the value of compliance and reduced false-alarm risk.

arguments.quote: The 406 MHz PLB is primarily intended to provide a distress and alerting capacity for use by the general public in life threatening situations in a remote environment after all other means of notifying SAR responders (e.g., telephone, radio) have been exhausted.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that outdoor recreationists are aware of or willing to purchase the device, nor that they would pay a premium price.

arguments.quote: require mandatory registration of 406 MHz PLB with the NOAA, and require manufacturers of 406 MHz PLBs to comply with the Radio Technical Commission for Maritime Services (RTCM) Recommended Standards for 406 MHz Satellite PLBs.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that commercial fishing or recreational boating operators are aware of or willing to purchase the device, nor that they would pay a premium price.

arguments.name: Consumer vs B2B Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product pages for two versions: (1) Outdoor recreation-focused 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a portable emergency solution for remote activities; (2) Commercial fishing/recreational boating-focused 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a compliant, low-cost emergency solution for vessels. Participants are randomly assigned to view one version and then asked about purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?" ) and willingness to pay (open amount).
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults: 250 outdoor recreationists (hiking, camping, climbing) recruited via outdoor activity forums; 250 recreational boat/fishing operators recruited via marine industry newsletters. Stratify by age and gender to reflect typical user demographics.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and average willingness-to-pay (EUR) for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreationists exposed to the outdoor recreation version will show purchase intent ≥30% and willingness-to-pay ≥15% above the price of existing PLBs (e.g., €300).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Commercial fishing/recreational boating operators exposed to the B2B version will show purchase intent ≥30% and willingness-to-pay ≥15% above the price of existing PLBs (e.g., €300).

arguments.decision_rule: If outdoor recreation version meets both intent ≥30% and willingness-to-pay ≥15% thresholds, proceed with consumer-focused product development. If B2B version meets both thresholds, proceed with marine distributor partnership. If neither meets thresholds,

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer vs B2B purchase intent test to gather real demand data before committing resources. If the test meets the thresholds for the outdoor recreation version, proceed with a consumer-focused product; otherwise, maintain focus on B2B markets.

arguments.value_proposition: A reliable, low-cost 406 MHz distress beacon that provides emergency notification via satellite, addressing the specific safety needs of remote outdoor activities.
arguments.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 purchase‑intent test with 500 participants (250 outdoor recreationists, 250 recreational boat/fishing operators). Measure purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay against predefined thresholds.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a 406 MHz distress beacon in 2002.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent ≥ 30% and willingness‑to‑pay ≥ 15% above existing PLB prices for outdoor recreationists, proceed with a consumer product.
If the test shows purchase intent ≥ 30% and willingness‑to‑pay ≥ 15% above existing PLB prices for recreational boat/fishing operators, pursue a marine‑focused B2B partnership.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/military/marine product line into new segments (e.g., commercial fishing, yacht owners) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

Regulatory requirements (e.g., mandatory registration) do not hinder consumer adoption.
predictions: If ACR launches a consumer product, purchase intent among outdoor recreation participants will be at least 15% higher than a control group.

T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR sells beacons through emergency services procurement channels (e.g., government contracts, emergency management agencies) at volume prices, earning recurring revenue and brand credibility in critical safety applications.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current dealer‑based B2B model for farm and industrial equipment.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a convenient, time‑saving tool for yard work, leading to premium pricing for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking efficient yard care; Deere benefits by capturing higher margins through direct sales and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing suburban population and increasing disposable income make yard work a visible, valued activity; a tractor offers faster, less‑labor‑intensive results than hand tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors directly to consumers at retail prices, leveraging its existing dealer network to reach individual buyers and its tractor engineering for a differentiated offering.
assumptions: Suburban growth in the 1960s will increase demand for yard care tools.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting practical demand, using the existing dealer network. Begin with a limited test (e.g., 20 dealers offering a compact, lifestyle‑branded tractor) to validate demand before full rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer types).
3) No expansion: maintain current business model and focus on existing dealer network and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they perceive them as a practical, inexpensive tool for multiple tasks, and they can purchase them through existing dealer networks without a differentiated proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain a versatile, low‑cost device for yard work; Deere benefits by selling through its existing dealer network without new marketing channels.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing small‑garden households need a machine that can do multiple jobs; the low price and availability through dealers make the tractor attractive.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging existing relationships and inventory to reach individual buyers without additional investment.
assumptions: Small‑garden households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to afford a lawn and garden tractor.
Deere dealers are willing to stock and sell lawn and garden tractors.
Consumers trust Deere's brand for agricultural equipment and will extend that trust to lawn and garden products.
predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn and garden tractor, dealers will stock it and sales will increase relative to a control group of dealers not offering the product.
Consumer surveys from 1962 will show that a majority of small‑garden households consider a tractor a useful purchase for yard work.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Post‑World War II suburban growth creates a market of homeowners seeking to demonstrate modern, well‑maintained homes; a tractor is seen as a visible sign of progress and status.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by launching a differentiated consumer line, selling directly to homeowners through new channels (e.g., mail‑order, dedicated retail) and commanding higher margins.
assumptions: Suburban homeowners in 1962 have disposable income to afford a premium lawn and garden product.
Deere can create a differentiated brand image that resonates with suburban values.
Consumers are willing to purchase a tractor as a lifestyle item rather than just a functional tool.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated consumer line with lifestyle branding, sales will exceed those of a comparable functional model sold through the same dealer network.
Surveys from 1962 will show that a significant portion of homeowners cite status or lifestyle as a reason for purchasing a lawn and garden tractor.

X1.method: Randomly select 20 John Deere dealers in the Midwest (10 in Illinois, 10 in neighboring states) and offer them a limited‑edition, differentiated consumer lawn and garden tractor (e.g., a compact model with lifestyle branding) at a price 15% above the standard 1962 model. Dealers can choose to stock the product or not. Track whether each dealer accepts the offer and the number of units they commit to sell.
X1.sample: 20 independent John Deere dealers in the Midwest
X1.measure: Number of dealers that accept the offer and the total units committed to sell (in units).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 15 dealers will accept the offer and commit to sell at least 150 units, indicating practical demand and existing dealer network willingness.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Fewer than 10 dealers will accept the offer and commit to sell fewer than 100 units, indicating limited status‑driven demand and dealer reluctance to stock a differentiated product.

final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens who need a versatile, inexpensive tool for yard work.
final.value_proposition: A lawn and garden tractor that is easy to use, economical to maintain, and sold through existing dealer networks, addressing the practical needs of small‑garden households.
